analysis.title: Ruminations - Macro, Micro, Markets
key_insights: Nasdaq fell 5% on the week and tech lost $5 trillion of market cap over three weeks, yet most of the S&P rose over the last month. Concentration is rotating into breadth through a positioning unwind and a chase for defensive and under-owned sectors.
On the day Alphabet lost $500bn of market cap the S&P fell only 30bps, offset by healthcare, real estate and staples outperformance. Russell beat the S&P and the S&P ex-AI beat the S&P last week.

Gross exposure has been very hard to carry for three weeks. Spreads such as software vs semis, value vs growth, small vs large cap, cyclicals vs defensives and crowding vs breadth are all difficult to manage, and the dividend yield and valuation factors sit in the 90th and 80th percentiles.

Q3 results were mixed. Google missed on revenue and EPS with negative free cash flow and had its worst one-day move in 20 years. Amazon had AWS growth of 39% and a record operating margin but trailing 12 month FCF turned negative and capex is signalled higher. Intel gave a weak Q4 guide and a cash burn warning for FY26 and fell the most on record.
SOX fell 7% on Friday and closed below its 200 day moving average for the first time in a year. Semis forward P/E is back to AI-cycle lows at about 16x.

Demand is not the issue. Google cloud doubled, Azure grew 48% and AWS grew at its fastest rate in 5 years. The concern is the cost and time to a return as hyperscalers move from cash-generating to cash-spending businesses, with combined FCF of the big 4 at $26bn and growing use of debt and equity financing.

The author questions why both spenders and recipients of AI capex are being sold together, since one company's capex is another's revenue. The week marked a shift from rewarding ambition to demanding returns and cash flow over capex.

Headline index drawdowns since 2020 were Covid -25%, Russia/Ukraine -24%, 2024 growth scare -11%, Liberation Day 2025 -12%, AI disruption and Iran conflict 2026 -10%, and the latest AI doubts -13%. The index was up 70% from trough to peak coming into last week.

Credit is flashing a warning. The B vs CCC spread has hit the 8% level fewer than 5 times since 1996, and each time the S&P was at least 11.5% below its 52 week high. The S&P was within 2% of that high coming into last week.

The author calls it a stealth bear market. The S&P is 3% from its all-time high, but the Mag 7 has lost $4 trillion since October 15 and 60% of S&P constituents are in bear market territory. Earnings were not 'good enough' for the first time the author can remember.

Peak-to-date drawdowns in AI and momentum names include Applovin -65%, Western Digital -52%, Oracle -50%, Arm -49%, ServiceNow -37%, Intel -35%, Broadcom -31%, Marvell -30%, Alphabet -28% and Meta -22%.

The market appears to have decided Google's core search business is under threat from AI agents that do the searching in an ad-free environment. The author argues it was foreseeable that high-return hyperscaler businesses would be challenged.
Google and Meta each earned around $200bn from advertising in 2025. The innovator's dilemma of doubling down on the status quo or pivoting may partly explain their capex ramp.

Fiscal pressure is building as governments are caught between populism and fiscal prudence. Issuance is driven by new spending, debt servicing, inflation and risk premium, and if absorption by savings and foreign capital falls short, tax rises or spending cuts become necessary.

Political tail risks remain. Brazil rallied 15% into the election and then sold off nearly 30% after an unexpected Lula win. Israel's election left coalition outcomes unclear, unrest continues in France and US midterms are ahead. The UK budget passed without disrupting Gilts.

The author sees UK equities improving on relative political stability, low but growing growth, defensive safe havens, a lack of tech now seen as a positive, and the Arm and Flutter drawdowns showing US listings are not a cure-all.

Cyber names have outperformed the S&P year to date, with Okta +155%, Fortinet +138%, CrowdStrike +124%, Palo Alto +116% and the HACK ETF +56%. The author ties growing cyber risk to AI and technology change.
earnings_insights: Alphabet reported Q3: revenue and EPS missed (no figures given in the note), free cash flow was negative, and the stock had its worst one-day move in 20 years, erasing about $500bn of market cap. Google cloud revenue doubled.

Amazon reported Q3: AWS growth of 39%, the fastest in 5 years, and its highest operating margin ever. Trailing 12 month FCF turned negative and the print signalled higher capex next year. Long-term debt rose from $66bn to $173bn in 9 months.
Intel reported Q3: weak Q4 guide and a cash burn warning for FY26. The stock had its largest one-day decline on record.
Microsoft Azure grew 48% in its latest report, cited as evidence that demand remains solid.
Meta raised financing last week, cited as part of hyperscalers funding capex with debt and equity as well as cash.
The big 4 hyperscalers' combined free cash flow was $26bn, a fraction of prior levels. More Mag 7 earnings are still ahead.

macro_indicators.reading: rising CPI, PPI and PCE inflation
macro_indicators.interpretation: Rising inflation, a sticky high US 10 year yield and $100 plus oil form the macro backdrop for the equity sell-off.

crypto_views: The author cites the weekend Binance hack as an example of growing cyber risk that comes with AI and technology innovation.
risk_factors: Hyperscaler capex ROI and funding risk, with FCF turning negative and rising reliance on debt and equity issuance.
Credit stress, with the B vs CCC spread at a level that has historically preceded S&P drawdowns of at least 11.5%.
Oil above $100 and possible Iran escalation around the midterms.
Sticky high US 10 year yield and rising CPI, PPI and PCE inflation.
Political tail risks including US midterms, France and post-election coalition uncertainty in Israel.
Fiscal pressure and growing sovereign issuance competing for capital.
AI disruption of the search and advertising economics of incumbent platforms.
vol_and_positioning: Index-level volatility looks calm while volatility beneath the surface is very different, with key spreads hard to manage.
Gross exposure has been extremely hard to carry for three weeks, with a positioning unwind and a chase for defensive and under-owned segments.
The dividend yield factor and valuation factor are trading in the 90th and 80th percentiles.
S&P ex-AI beat the S&P and Russell beat the S&P last week, a reversal of concentration toward breadth.
SOX is below its 200 day moving average for the first time in a year.
geopolitical: Investors are nervous about Iran escalation before or after the US midterms and about Iran next steps as a catalyst.
Market-implied odds of a Democratic sweep in the US midterms rose to 72%.
Israel election results are in but coalition and government formation remain unclear.
Brazil's unexpected Lula win and Bolsonaro departure triggered a near 30% sell-off after a 15% pre-election rally.
The UK budget passed without major disruption to the Gilt market.

tension_points.bull_case: Demand is solid. Google cloud doubled, Azure grew 48%, AWS grew at its fastest rate in 5 years and chip demand is rock solid. The base case remains that AI will change everything, and one company's capex is another's revenue.
tension_points.bear_case: Hyperscalers are turning from cash printing to cash spending machines. Combined FCF of the big 4 is $26bn, Amazon's long-term debt rose from $66bn to $173bn in 9 months, and investors now want returns over ambition.

tension_points.theme: index calm vs stealth bear market
tension_points.bull_case: The S&P is only about 3% below its all-time high and most of the index is up over the last month, with defensive sectors offsetting tech losses.
tension_points.bear_case: The Mag 7 has lost $4 trillion since October 15 and 60% of the S&P is in bear market territory. The B vs CCC spread hit the 8% trigger that has preceded S&P drawdowns of at least 11.5%.
tension_points.what_invalidates: The bull view is invalidated if the S&P falls to 11.5% or more below its 52 week high, the smallest drawdown seen on prior occasions when the B vs CCC spread hit 8%.
